newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Central Africa rebels detain leader over truce.
newsitem.headline: Central Africa rebels detain leader over truce.

text.p: Army mutineers in the Central African Republic have detained their leader for signing a deal extending a truce in the capital Bangui, rebels said on Monday.

They said Captain Anicet Saulet was seized by soldiers who said the one-month extension he agreed to was longer than he had been authorised to sign. He was being held at a rebel base in Bangui's Petevo district.
"Captain Saulet betrayed the military in signing a truce of 30 days whereas the soldiers insisted on 15 days," mutiny coordinator Sergeant Roger Kongbossomo told Reuters.
Separately, hundreds of residents in rebel strongholds in Bangui's southern districts marched to demand a quick and permanent end to the mutiny that has disrupted their lives.
Witnesses said some demostrators carried spears, bows and arrows and stones, saying they were ready to confront rebels.
Marchers said the accord was not enough to end the tribal feuding that followed the mutiny which started on November 16.
Despite the signing of the accord on Sunday extending an earlier 15-day truce, occasional gunfire echoed across the riverside capital during the night.
The government and mutineers extended the ceasefire to January 23 and agreed to form a joint security commission.

Thousands of Bangui residents had fled the capital ahead of the expiration date of the previous ceasefire brokered by four African presidents. A third of the city's population of 600,000 left, according to some estimates.

Both sides agreed to refrain from any acts or statements likely to compromise national unity during the truce period, but barricades dividing the city into rebel and government held districts remained in place.

The accord was signed by President Ange-Felix Patasse, rebel leader Captain Anicet Saulet, mediator General Amadou Toumani Toure, the former military ruler of Mali, and French ambassador Jean-Marc Simon, who took part in the negotiations.

French troops based in the former colony under bilateral accords helped keep President Ange-Felix Patasse in power during a violent mutiny last May and have been backing loyalist forces in the latest revolt.
Mutineers with pay grievances later started demanding that Patasse step down. Patasse was elected 1993 and has dismissed calls for his resignation, backed by the opposition, as unconstitutional.
In Paris, France welcomed the new accord and said the opposing parties would use the truce period to work on lasting solutions to ensure national reconciliation.
The mutiny has turned into bloody feuding between his Baya tribe and Yakomas who dominate the ranks of rebel soldiers.
